strengths: Rigorous experimental methodology with proper compute-matched baselines and multiple ablations demonstrating careful scientific practice
Honest discussion of limitations including task-dependent benefits and perplexity-performance disconnect, showing genuine engagement with results
Notable improvements on specific reasoning-heavy benchmarks (ARC-Easy: +5%, PIQA: +2.1%), suggesting targeted benefits for knowledge-intensive tasks
Practical, implementable framework combining curriculum learning with progressive stacking, useful for resource-constrained pretraining
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks and two independent model scales (GPT-2 Small and LLaMA-1B) with detailed experimental documentation
weaknesses: Limited overall novelty: combines established techniques (curriculum learning, progressive stacking, layer freezing) without fundamental new insights or theoretical contribution
Modest average improvements (1% at GPT-2 Small, 2.17% at LLaMA-1B) without statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple runs reported

Unexplained perplexity-performance disconnect: randomized baseline achieves better language modeling perplexity but worse downstream performance at LLaMA scale, raising questions about what CGLS optimizes for

Inconsistent curriculum designs across scales (TinyStories→BookCorpus→DCLM vs. stratified DCLM) make it difficult to isolate whether improvements stem from progressive stacking principle or specific curriculum design
Task-dependent results with no improvements on HellaSwag and LAMBADA, limiting generality and providing no guidance on when practitioners should apply CGLS
Critical hyperparameter sensitivity (N1=N/2 crucial) combined with admitted limited exploration due to budget constraints suggests potential fragility of the approach
Limited scope and scalability: maximum 1.2B parameters, no evaluation of wall-clock time or actual compute savings, uncertain generalization beyond this scale for modern standards
Insufficient mechanistic explanation of why synchronizing model and data complexity should help; cognitive development analogy is intuitive but not rigorously justified or formalized

strengths: Systematic compute-matched evaluation with multiple well-chosen baselines (randomized, curricularized, layer-scaling only, MIDAS)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two parameter scales (124M and 1.2B) with diverse downstream tasks (PIQA, ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, LAMBADA, Pile)
Ablation studies examining different starting depths (N₁ = 3, 6, 8, 10) to understand design choices
Honest discussion of limitations, including acknowledgment that not all tasks benefit equally and the perplexity-generalization disconnect
Clear presentation with good motivation from cognitive development analogy and well-designed figures
Proper compute budget matching (FLOPs) across methods enables fair comparison
weaknesses: Critical unexplained phenomenon: randomized baseline achieves lower perplexity (20.83 vs 25.34) than CGLS at 1.2B scale yet performs worse on downstream tasks; this perplexity-generalization disconnect is acknowledged but not investigated, undermining confidence in results
Limited novelty: straightforward combination of two existing techniques (curriculum learning and progressive stacking) without methodological innovation

Modest and inconsistent improvements with no significance testing: typically 1-2% on average across benchmarks; claimed 5% on ARC-Easy is against weak baseline; LAMBADA and HellaSwag show negligible gains

Curriculum design is entirely dataset/task-specific rather than principled: different curricula at two scales (synthetic→general→diverse vs general→domain→specialized) with hand-crafted mixture weights; no framework for generalizing to new domains

Hyperparameter tuning appears underspecified: the finding that N₁ = N/2 is optimal seems fortunate rather than principled; authors acknowledge inability to exhaustively tune due to compute constraints
Missing ablations on critical design choices: two-phase training for new layers (initialize on balanced data, then curriculum) is not justified; stage FLOP allocations (20%/20%/20%/40%) not ablated
Scale limitations: only tested up to 1.2B parameters; scalability claims are overstated given only two scales
MMLU results near chance (25%); STEM improvements marginal (26.55% vs 24.84%) using non-standard metrics (PMI, token-normalized accuracy)
MIDAS baseline reimplemented from pseudocode without released code—difficult to verify; layer-scaling only baseline sometimes performs comparably to CGLS, questioning the value of curriculum
No statistical significance testing despite small improvements (1-2%); single runs reported without error bars or confidence intervals
No mechanistic analysis of what makes the approach work or how representations evolve across stages; no learning curves or visualization of complexity differences
Curriculum stratification at 1.2B depends on GPT-4o labeling, introducing external dependency and reproducibility concerns; code not released
BookCorpus used despite acknowledged legal ambiguity regarding copyright

strengths: Well-motivated empirical contribution: convincingly shows that progressive stacking + curriculum learning together outperform either approach alone, with practical implications for compute-efficient pretraining
Rigorous experimental design: compute-matched baselines, systematic ablations over starting depths (N₁=3,6,8,10), comprehensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks and per-domain analysis
Clear presentation and reproducibility: detailed experimental setup, well-designed figures, honest discussion of limitations, appropriate dataset licenses and broader impacts
Valuable insight that synchronization is needed: MIDAS-style progressive stacking alone underperforms on knowledge-intensive tasks; paper shows why and proposes practical solution
Staged training methodology is well-motivated: freezing earlier layers during new layer initialization preserves learned representations and aligns with recent findings from Kumar et al.
weaknesses: Severe scale limitations: results only at 124M and 1.2B parameters with unclear generalization to modern scales (7B+); different curricula needed at different scales suggests approach lacks principled methodology

Curriculum design is ad-hoc and opaque: TinyStories→BookCorpus→DCLM choices appear hand-crafted; mixture weights manually tuned; N₁=N/2 heuristic empirically validated but lacks theoretical justification; no principled procedure for designing curricula on new datasets

Perplexity-downstream disconnect unexplained: at 1.2B scale, randomized baseline has significantly lower perplexity (20.83 vs 25.34) yet worse downstream performance—raises concerns about evaluation validity or overfitting to curriculum without improving general language modeling
Modest improvements with inconsistent task coverage: 1.0% average at GPT-2, 2.17% at 1.2B; strongest on specific benchmarks (ARC-Easy: 5%) but no gains on LAMBADA/HellaSwag, limiting generalizability

Compute budget effects unclear: results only under constrained budgets (0.7B and 2.5B tokens) substantially below Chinchilla-optimal; unclear whether benefits persist with realistic training or optimal allocations

Limited theoretical insight: primarily empirical contribution with no mechanistic understanding of why synchronization works; cognitive development motivation is intuitive but not rigorously justified

Data stratification robustness concerns: DistilBERT classifier achieves >90% accuracy leaving ~10% error; GPT-4o-mini labeling introduces potential bias; no sensitivity analysis on classification quality

strengths: Rigorous compute-matched experimental methodology with multiple baselines (randomized, curricularized, layer-scaling only, MIDAS) and ablation studies on key hyperparameters
Consistent improvements on knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks (PIQA +2.1%, ARC-Easy +5%) validated through multi-seed experiments showing lower variance than baselines at small scales
Comprehensive evaluation spanning multiple scales (100M to 1.2B parameters, 2.5B to 20B tokens), downstream tasks, and domain shift scenarios (DCLM to code)
Clear isolation of contribution through ablations: demonstrates that layer stacking alone fails, but succeeds when paired with data curriculum
Honest discussion of limitations including perplexity-performance divergence and tasks where method provides minimal benefit (HellaSwag, LAMBADA)
Well-written paper with reproducible setup: detailed experimental hyperparameters, data curricula specifications, and comprehensive appendix
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines two existing techniques (curriculum learning and progressive stacking) in straightforward manner; two-phase training from Kumar et al. (2022); similar ideas explored in concurrent work (Phi-3, MiniCPM midtraining, Gururangan et al. 2020 continued pretraining)

Concerning perplexity-performance disconnect at 2.5B tokens: CGLS achieves higher perplexity (25.34 vs 20.83) than randomized baseline despite better downstream accuracy; divergence only resolves at 20B tokens, raising questions about whether approach learns better representations or exploits task-specific biases

Ad-hoc curriculum design with no principled methodology: different curricula at different scales (TinyStories/BookCorpus/DCLM vs. DistilBERT stratification); no ablation on curriculum ordering or design principles; severely limits generalization to new domains

Modest improvements with high variance: average gains 1-1.7%, CGLS shows higher variance than baselines (±1.42% vs ±0.28% for PIQA); inconsistent across tasks (HellaSwag, LAMBADA show minimal gains); lacks statistical significance testing

Limited experimental scale: only tested up to 1.2B parameters with 2.5B tokens; modern pretraining operates at 10B-70B+ parameters with 1T+ tokens; benefits likely diminish at production scales; claims about 'scaling' overstated

Critical hyperparameter sensitivity: starting depth found to be 'particularly important' with narrow optimal range (N1=N/2); different optimal configurations across scales suggest instability; no principled guidance for new scenarios
Suspicious MIDAS baseline performance: reimplemented from pseudocode with no verification; performs worse than layer-scaling alone, which seems anomalous and questions comparison fairness

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: no representation analysis or probing of what features emerge at different curriculum stages; no investigation of whether early layers learn 'simpler' patterns; limited insight into why approach works

strengths: Well-executed experimental methodology with compute-matched baselines, multiple scales, ablations, and stability checks
Clear presentation with intuitive figures and comprehensive appendix supporting reproducibility
Honest discussion of limitations, including acknowledgment that not all tasks benefit equally
Extension to Chinchilla-optimal 20B token scale showing consistent improvements across all benchmarks
Breadth of evaluation including perplexity analysis across Pile subsets, domain-shift experiments, and stability analysis
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements of 1-2% average with inconsistent gains across tasks; some benchmarks show minimal benefit (e.g., HellaSwag 34.65% vs 34.20%)

Unexplained perplexity-downstream performance disconnect at primary scale (worse perplexity 25.34 vs 20.83 but better downstream 39.08% vs 37.38%); explanation via scaling laws is hand-wavy rather than mechanistic
Misleading 'compute-efficient' framing: compute budget is matched not reduced, wall-clock time is actually higher (5h53m vs 5h39m), and checkpoint loading overhead undermines efficiency claims
Significant hyperparameter sensitivity requiring scale-specific tuning (starting depth N₁=N/2, stage budgets, curriculum weights differ between scales); no principled method for new domains
Limited experimental scale with sub-optimal token-to-parameter ratios (2.08× at 1B scale vs 20× Chinchilla-optimal); main claims rely on underprovisioned experiments
Data stratification depends on external DistilBERT classifier trained on GPT-4o-labeled data, raising reproducibility and generalization concerns
Lack of theoretical understanding for key design choices: why N/2 is optimal, why curriculum + stacking synergize, why perplexity diverges from downstream performance
Inconsistent baseline behavior where layer-scaling-only sometimes underperforms randomized baseline, suggesting incomplete understanding of method interactions

strengths: Well-motivated approach combining progressive layer stacking with curriculum learning, drawing compelling analogy from cognitive development
Rigorous experimental design with proper compute-matched baselines that isolate contributions (randomized, curricularized, layer-scaling only, MIDAS)
Key insight effectively demonstrated: layer scaling alone underperforms on knowledge tasks; curriculum alone is adequate; synchronized combination is optimal
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple scales (100M to 1.2B parameters, up to 20B tokens) demonstrating scalability and robustness
Thorough ablation studies on critical hyperparameters (starting depth, compute allocation) with clear findings (N/2 sweet spot)
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, data curriculum specifications, and comprehensive appendix enable reproduction
Honest discussion of limitations (task-specific gains, perplexity disconnect, design choices) without overclaiming
Extended experiments demonstrate generality (domain-shift to code pretraining shows 2x improvement in pass@8)
weaknesses: Modest task-dependent improvements (1.0%-3.9%) with significant variation; minimal gains on LAMBADA and HellaSwag (~0.5%)
Limited scale relative to modern standards (max 1.2B parameters, 20B tokens); claims about scalability rest on single 20B-token experiment
Perplexity-downstream performance disconnect unresolved at 2.5B tokens; explanation invoking depth importance is post-hoc and unsatisfying; only resolved at 20B tokens
Data curriculum construction is ad-hoc and labor-intensive; requires domain knowledge and manual design; DistilBERT classifier trained on only 20k samples
Higher optimization variance for CGLS across seeds (Table 7: some benchmarks show ~1.5-2.4% standard error vs. ~0.3% baseline)
Implementation overhead not negligible (2.5% wall-clock time increase despite FLOP matching); optimizer state resets add engineering complexity
Limited technical novelty: curriculum learning and progressive stacking are established; two-phase training from Kumar et al. (2022); main contribution is combination (incremental)
Narrow task evaluation biased toward reasoning/knowledge (PIQA, ARC); limited coverage of diverse tasks (no translation, summarization, generation tasks)
Insufficient exploration of curriculum sensitivity; single curriculum design per scale tested; generalization to other complexity metrics unclear
